entries.claim_value: Side B in Höpfner: when the town was abandoned the garrison, the 3rd battalion of the King's regiment, 3 invalid companies and 65 artillerymen, not over 900 men strong after deducting the sick and unfit, withdrew into the citadel. There was powder for a little over 60 cartridges a man and 2475 rounds for 71 guns.
entries.author_rationale: Side B's history, read from the page image of p. 129. The garrison was the place's own, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'when on 22 October no workers had yet come in, and the enemy had already crossed the Elbe'; 'the town was abandoned and the garrison — the 3rd battalion of the King's regiment, 3 invalid companies and 65 artillerymen, not over 900 men strong after deducting the sick and unfit — withdrew to the citadel'; 'as the promised powder had not arrived from Berlin, there were only 142 hundredweight of powder, from which a little over 60 cartridges per man and 2475 rounds for 71 guns could be made up'.

entries.claim_value: Side B prepared the fortress late: only on 17 October did the Ober-Kriegs-Kollegium order it made ready against a violent attack, and only on the 20th did the government call up carpenters and workers from the country; for want of time the defence was confined to the main rampart and Fort Preussen, and the outworks were abandoned as wholly decayed. The governor answered the first summons that he would defend the fortress to the utmost, but then drafted terms to hand it over the next morning with free withdrawal and all marks of honour; the capitulation's first article asked free exit with arms and baggage to West and North Prussia or Silesia, and its fifth at least 24 hours for the troops to settle their affairs.
entries.author_rationale: Höpfner from the page images of pp. 216 and 218, the capitulation's articles from the page image of p. 525. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'only on 17 October had the order been issued by the Ober-Kriegs-Kollegium to make the fortress ready against a violent attack, and only on the 20th did the government summon the necessary carpenters and workers from the country'; 'for shortness of time the defensive arrangements had to be confined to the main rampart and Fort Preussen, and the outworks in front abandoned because of their wholly decayed state'; as in claim side-b-command for the governor's answer and his draft; the capitulation, as in claim capitulation for art. 1; 'art. 5. The Prussian troops will be granted at least 24 hours to arrange their affairs'.

No passage read gives a loss for side A, and Bodart prints none. Höpfner says the fortress's batteries drove the enemy back emphatically after it entered the bridgehead on 31 October, but gives no French loss, and Bodart says the garrison surrendered without striking a blow. No loss is stated, so it is left unknown, not set to zero.

entries.claim_value: Krauss says Dupont's division set out from Albeck toward Ulm at 11 a.m. on 11 October. Baraguey d'Hilliers, acknowledging Ney's orders, wrote that his dragoons on foot were somewhat dispersed and had marched or bivouacked all night in frightful weather, the roads were broken up and the artillery would have great difficulty arriving. Of Dupont's guns a 4-pounder was under repair; at Haslach the French artillery, much inferior to the enemy's, was partly dismounted and several pieces had their horses killed, the snow and rain of several days having made the ground extremely difficult. During the action enemy cavalry reached the division's rear, carried off the baggage and plundered the park, and on the retreat the division lost all its 12- and 8-pounders, overturned crossing ditches.
entries.author_rationale: Movement and means as the sources report them; no supply return was inspected. The late start followed the late delivery of Ney's orders (claim side-a-support), so the phase is unresolved. English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'Dupont's division had set out from Albeck toward Ulm on 11 October at 11 a.m.'; Baraguey d'Hilliers, 'the troops are somewhat dispersed and will arrive rather late at their cantonments; they have marched or bivouacked all night in frightful weather; the roads are broken up and the artillery will have great difficulty in arriving'; 'a 4-pounder is under repair on 11 October'; 'our artillery, too inferior to the enemy's, was partly dismounted; several pieces had their horses killed; the snow and the rain, which had prevailed for several days, having made the ground extremely difficult, this inferiority was felt still more'; 'during the action the enemy cavalry moved onto the rear, carried off the baggage and plundered the objects of the park'; Krauss, 'where, coming upon the train of Dupont's division, it caused great confusion'; 'on the retreat the division lost all the twelve- and eight-pounders, which overturned in crossing ditches and could not be righted again'.
No passage read gives side A's loss at Trochtelfingen or in Fauconnet's attack on the convoy's tail, and Bodart prints none. Unknown, not zero.

entries.claim_value: Bodart describes Eschenau as a village in Bavaria, Middle Franconia, 10 km northeast of Nuremberg. Beyond Nuremberg the Austrian baggage was entering the Reichswald forest on the Gräfenberg road; the Austrian cavalry stood in line in front of Heroldsberg as the French came out of the wood, guns were put into battery on the height of Geschaid, and the decisive charge came near Forth. Krauss says side B's infantry had marched without a break in pouring rain.
entries.author_rationale: Ground from Bodart, Krauss and the page images, with the record's and Alombert and Colin's passages on the forest, Heroldsberg and Geschaid seen in the OCR; no map was inspected. English renderings (ours): Bodart, 'village in Bavaria, Middle Franconia, 10 km northeast of Nuremberg'; the record, 'it was only after having made ... leagues and when we were at Nuremberg that we discovered his infantry in the plain and the tail of his baggage entering the forest of Reichswald, following the road to Gräfenberg'; 'coming out of the wood they had to fight the enemy cavalry, which was in line in front of the village of Heroldsberg'; Alombert and Colin, as in claim side-b-command; the record on Forth, as in claim side-a-command; Krauss, as in claim krauss-side-b.

entries.claim_value: Side A was the pursuer: Klein summoned Werneck's corps, its night march toward Öttingen turned back on meeting French troops, and Fauconnet's chasseurs attacked the tail of the convoy as far as Trochtelfingen until the parley stopped them. Side B took position on a plateau and then capitulated; no passage read describes it attacking at Trochtelfingen.
entries.author_rationale: The pursuit was set by Murat's orders of the 17th and the action at Neresheim (B365b); the passages read show no new decision to attack at Trochtelfingen, where the summons and the negotiation decided the engagement, so the posture is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): Alombert and Colin, 'General Fauconnet was charging at the same time the tail of the convoy with his two regiments of chasseurs, but General Werneck's capitulation put an end to the fight'; the report and the journal, as in claims side-a-forces and side-b-command.

No passage read gives a loss for side A, and Bodart prints none. Belliard says the governor greeted the French with a few cannon shots, and Höpfner has the garrison fire on enemy horsemen riding too boldly forward (claim side-b-command), but neither gives a French loss. No loss is stated, so it is left unknown, not set to zero.

entries.claim_value: Side A's aims: Krauss says the Emperor's orders brought about the capture of Memmingen, and that on Napoleon's order of the 13th Soult sent two divisions on to Ochsenhausen while the 2nd and Walther's dragoons kept Memmingen invested; Soult meant the corps to intercept the Biberach road and complete the encirclement of the enemy in Ulm. Soult explains that he took terms rather than attack in form because it was advantageous for the Emperor's operations to have a half-fortified post as a place of arms, the garrison would have obliged him to leave a regiment behind, and the enemy would have had a support at Memmingen; afterwards he wrote that the conquest took a support from the Austrian army, opened a sure communication and had not delayed his march.
entries.author_rationale: Aims set from above and Soult's own reasons, read from the page images and his letter (OCR). English renderings (ours): Krauss, 'the Emperor's orders brought about two important events on 14 October: the capture of Memmingen and the action of Elchingen'; Soult, 'from where I proposed to direct them on Laupheim so as to intercept the Biberach road and entirely surround the enemy army in Ulm'; 'I would no doubt have forced this garrison to surrender at discretion, had I had more time to attack it in form, but I thought it advantageous for the operations Your Majesty proposes that there should be a half-fortified post'; 'I also considered that this garrison, however weak it was, would have obliged me ... to leave a regiment behind, and moreover that the enemy would have had a support at Memmingen'; 'it can serve as a place of arms; it takes a support away from the Austrian army ... it opens to us a sure communication, and has not delayed our march'.

No passage read says what side A knew of side B's position or strength, or of Rohan's departure from Landeck. Moriggl's statement that Jellachich hurried to capitulate before the enemy learned of it is side B's expectation (claim side-b-information), and Victoires says Ney's corps had cut Jellachich off from the Tyrol (claim side-b-command) but not what Augereau knew of it. Unknown.

entries.claim_value: Hillinger acted without precise knowledge of the events at Caldiero (Angeli). After Masséna's retrograde movement and the massing of the French army on the spurs of the Monti Lessini he lost all connection to his left as well (Angeli); cut off, he could not believe himself completely abandoned (Koch). Rosenberg's order to fall back on Ala reached him shortly after he had repulsed the first attack, when it could no longer be carried out (Angeli); Koch says he received the order to withdraw at nine in the morning.
entries.author_rationale: Side B's information as both accounts give it, read from the page images. English renderings (ours): Angeli, as in claim side-b-command for his lack of knowledge and Rosenberg's order; as in claim pojano-ground for the lost connection; Koch, as in claim koch-side-a for 'unable to believe himself completely abandoned'; as in claim side-b-command for the order received at nine.

entries.claim_value: Murat decided to march on Neresheim instead of Aalen: he sent Fauconnet's chasseur brigade and the 1st hussars toward Aalen to attack and hold the Austrian corps presumed to be retreating on Ellwangen, while he himself went by Neresheim and Nördlingen, Klein's dragoon division at the head of the column. Before Neresheim General Klein decided to attack with his division alone. He placed some of his guns against the Austrian battery and the others to fire on the Austrian cavalry, sent a regiment over the bridge against the front of the Austrian cavalry and led others across the Egau west of the bridge toward Ohmenheim, and when he saw the Austrian cavalry on the march on the Ohmenheim road he ordered the charge. After Sinzendorf's surrender he sent a parlementaire to summon Werneck to have his troops lay down their arms, as they were surrounded.
entries.author_rationale: Decisions at the engagement from Murat's letter, an interested account, the dragoon division's journal and Krauss (OCR passages, except those read from the page images); the numbers of guns and regiments in Klein's dispositions were seen only in the OCR and are marked (OCR) below. English renderings (ours): Murat, 'as I had the honour to announce to Your Majesty, I decided to march on Neresheim instead of moving on Aalen. This course succeeded perfectly for me'; Krauss, 'on the 17th Murat directed Fauconnet's chasseur brigade by Bartholomä and Essingen to Aalen, the 1st hussar regiment by Heidenheim to Aalen; both had the task of attacking without pause and bringing to bay the Austrian corps presumed to be retreating on Ellwangen, so that Murat, who would advance by Neresheim and Nördlingen, might gain the time to get ahead of the Austrians'; the cavalry reserve's report, 'the Prince with the rest of his troops marched on Neresheim; the 1st dragoon division held the head of the column'; Murat, 'General Klein, arrived at 5 o'clock in front of Neresheim, found the enemy there, who had just taken up position. He did not hesitate to have him attacked; to form, charge him and overthrow him was the work of an instant'; Krauss, 'General Klein first placed three (OCR) of his guns opposite the Austrian battery; the two (OCR) other guns he posted west of height ... in such a way that they could take the Austrian cavalry under fire but were covered against the Austrian artillery'; 'two (OCR) dragoon regiments now advanced against Neresheim; one (OCR) regiment Klein directed over the bridge against the front of the Austrian cavalry, but with three (OCR) regiments General Klein went west of the bridge across the Egau and west of the ravine toward Ohmenheim'; 'when General Klein saw the Austrian cavalry on the march on the road to Ohmenheim, he gave the order to charge, direction the church of Ohmenheim. The Austrian cavalry was thrown back; Klein's wheeling left wing struck Austrian infantry and cut it off from Ohmenheim'; the journal, 'General Zinzendorf was taken with several officers, and more than ... men; but this was only part of the army corps of Field Marshal Baron Werneck, and General Klein, wishing to profit from the consternation of the enemy, at once sent to that general squadron commander Gobrecht, commanding the ... dragoon regiment, to summon him to have his troops lay down their arms, because they were surrounded'.

No passage read gives a loss for side A, and Bodart prints none. No passage read describes any fighting at Boldekow: in Höpfner the park's escort had left before the capitulation, which was negotiated through a French officer. No loss is stated, so it is left unknown, not set to zero.

entries.claim_value: Bodart names Marshal Prince Murat as side A's commander and Lieutenant-General Prince Bagration as side B's.
entries.author_rationale: Bodart's printed commanders. Both other accounts have Murat order the attack and Bagration command the Russian rearguard (claims side-a-command and side-b-command); in both, Lannes and Soult (Victoires) or the IV and V Corps (Schönhals) fought under Murat, and Kutusow, the army commander, had marched on with the main body. English rendering (ours): 'under Marshal Prince Murat over the Russians and Austrians (5,500 infantry, 1,500 cavalry, 12 guns) under Lieutenant-General Prince Bagration'.

entries.claim_value: Side B's troops in contact: the journal has Wrede overtake the enemy rearguard and, a little short of Parsdorf, attack a battalion of the Deutschmeister regiment in sight of an enemy corps drawn up in line; the enemy army stood in line behind Parsdorf on the height of Anzing. No source read gives a headcount for the rearguard or for the corps in line.
entries.author_rationale: What the passages say was engaged, read from the page image; a strength for the engaged troops is missing, not zero. English renderings (ours): 'a little short of Parsdorf, the lieutenant general attacked, in sight of an enemy corps drawn up in line, a battalion of the Deutschmeister regiment'; 'the enemy army being drawn up in line behind Parsdorf, on the height of Anzing'.

No passage read gives side B's loss in the siege, and Bodart prints none. Colletta says that the closer the fighting came the deadlier it was and that hunger made the castle surrender (claims bodart-losses and bodart-winner); both histories send the garrison to Sicily under the capitulation. Unknown, not zero.

entries.claim_value: Both sides attacked. Davout reported that, debouching from Kösen, he found the enemy a quarter of a league off, marching to seize that debouch himself, and that the battle was engaged at once. Höpfner calls it, on both sides, a matter of dispositions after a chance encounter ('Rencontre'), both being surprised by running into a considerable opponent; the heads of both armies met at Hassenhausen, which the French occupied, and the division Gudin and the Prussian division Schmettau reached it at about the same time (the last OCR). The Prussians attacked: General Blücher's cavalry attacked the French infantry at Hassenhausen and was repulsed by the squares; the King ordered the division Schmettau to attack, and Schmettau's and Wartensleben's divisions attacked Hassenhausen but could not take it, the Duke having called on a grenadier battalion to take the village when he was shot; Prince Wilhelm's cavalry charged Morand's division, which received it in square (OCR). The French attacked: while Gudin's division held at Hassenhausen, Friant's went on turning the enemy, advancing between Spielberg and Zeckwar against the Prussian left; Davout sent Morand's division against the King's last effort to break the French left, and Morand outflanked the Prussian army and took it in flank; Davout then had the centre advance (OCR); at the end General Petit, ordered to attack the last Prussian position before Eckartsberga with 400 men, climbed the height with the bayonet without returning the fire and took 20 pieces of cannon.
entries.author_rationale: Coded both_attacked: a meeting engagement, in which the Prussian main attacks on Hassenhausen and the French main attacks by Friant's and Morand's divisions, the advance of the centre and the final attack before Eckartsberga fell on different parts of the field; neither side fought from a position taken up before the meeting, and the French defence of Hassenhausen and the Prussian reserve's stands before Eckartsberga were parts of a battle that both sides fought by attacking. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim. The meeting came from marches set by orders, Napoleon's to Davout and the Prussian disposition to take the post of Kösen (claims davout-decision and side-b-objectives), but the attacks were decided on the field by Davout, the Duke and the King, so the posture is tagged commander_created. English renderings (ours): Davout's report, 'Battle of Auerstädt'; 'Marshal Davout to the Emperor'; 'at the bivouac of Auerstädt, 14 October 1806' (p. 672); as in claim davout-decision for the debouch and the battle engaged at once (p. 672); Höpfner, 'it was a matter here, on both sides, of the arrangements after a Rencontre, for both parties were surprised by running into a considerable opponent' (p. 485); as in claim side-b-engaged for the first and third moments, and in claim hoepfner-side-a for Gudin and Schmettau; 'second moment. General Blücher attacks the enemy infantry at Hassenhausen with some cavalry and is repulsed. The enemy division Friant arrives'; 'the unshaken French squares received him coolly'; 'the King gave the division Schmettau the order to attack, which was begun in echelons from the left wing'; as in claim side-b-command for the Duke's wound (OCR); the journal, '[rein]forced by another numerous corps of cavalry, at whose head was Prince Wilhelm of Prussia'; 'the Prince charged the division Morand several times, but all the units, formed in square, received him coolly with cries of Vive l'Empereur!'; 'the division Gudin was defending itself with advantage level with Hassenhausen, while General Friant with the greater part of his division continued to turn the enemy, advanced between Spielberg and Zeckwar, and was already troubling the Prussians' left flank with a well placed and well directed artillery'; as in claim side-a-command for the King's last effort, Morand and the centre; '[Morand] outflanks and takes the Prussian army in flank; at the same time General Friant, placed likewise on the heights to the right of Poppel, was already outflanking the enemy's left wing' (OCR); the journal, 'extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd army corps' (p. 673); as in claim side-a-command for the last division and Petit's orders (OCR and p. 682); 'General Petit received the fire of the Prussian artillery and that of the musketry without replying; his troops climbed the hill with the bayonet forward, while General Grandeau arrived on the right of this hill with the greater part of the 111th, followed by General Friant and his division'; 'the enemy abandoned this fine and last position with such haste that he left 20 pieces of cannon in the power of General Petit' (p. 682).

entries.claim_value: Bodart names Napoleon I as side A's commander and Lieutenant General Count Ostermann as side B's. In Höpfner Ostermann commanded the 2nd Division and held the Wkra from Borkowo to its mouth; the army was General Bennigsen's, and Field Marshal Kaminskoi, who arrived at Pultusk on 21 December, drove Bennigsen to Nowemiasto and ordered all the troops to advance against the Wkra; the major general's letter of 25 December says that the field marshal commanding the Russian army in chief was at Nasielsk. Napoleon was on the field: he arrived at Okunin at 9 in the morning of the 23rd (Höpfner), at the entrenched camp between 9 and 10 (the journal), and dictated the order of attack (claim napoleon-decision).
entries.author_rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; Höpfner and Foucart from the page images (Höpfner pp. 23, 24, 82-84 and 88; Foucart pp. 390, 439 and 440). The commands were set before the action, so the claim is tagged inherited; Napoleon's and Davout's decisions on the field are in claims side-a-command and napoleon-decision, and Ostermann's in claim side-b-command. English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'Gen.-Lt.' is General-Leutnant, 'Gf.' Graf and 'M.' Mann in Bodart's list of abbreviations; Höpfner, 'first, there stood ready to advance on the Russian frontier on 1 November the army of General of Cavalry v. Bennigsen, which, according to the report handed in to the King by the Prussian General Chlebowski, posted to the headquarters,' (p. 23); '[report] of 23 October consisted of the 2nd, 3rd, 4th and 6th Divisions and had the following composition:' (p. 24); 'General Bennigsen had, as has been shown, very soon given up the offensive and decided to await the French in a central position at Pultusk, at the same time defending the line of the Wkra with suitable forces'; 'General Ostermann with the rest of the 2nd Division held the Wkra from Borkowo downstream to its mouth in the Narew, and that river upstream from the mouth, having relieved the greater part of the 6th Division that day;'; 'on 21 December Field Marshal Kaminskoi at last arrived at Pultusk on a peasant cart'; 'with violent reproaches he drove' (p. 83); 'General Bennigsen to Nowemiasto, and ordered all the troops to advance against the Wkra' (p. 84); 'Napoleon in person went to Jablonna on the 22nd and arrived at Okunin on the 23rd at 9 in the morning'; the journal, 'night combat at Czarnowo'; '(extract from the journal of marches and operations of the 3rd corps)'; 'the Emperor left Warsaw on the 23rd at 3 in the morning so as to be at daybreak at Marshal Davout's bridge on the Narew. He arrived between 9 and 10 in the morning at the entrenched camp. He began by visiting the entrenched camp; then, in the presence of the Russians who lined the left bank, he reconnoitred the Wkra from Pomichowo to the two arms of this river at its mouth' (p. 390); the major general, 'the major general to Marshal Lannes'; 'Slostowo, 25 December 1806'; 'he had a division of about 15,000 men to defend the right bank of the Wkra and the bridge of Pomichowo; another division of the same strength defended Kolozomb, with its point of support at Nowemiasto. The division that defended the Wkra was beaten at Pomichowo, Czarnowo and Nasielsk, where the field marshal commanding the Russian army in chief was'.

entries.claim_value: Bodart names Marshal Augereau as side A's commander and FML Baron Jellachich as side B's.
entries.author_rationale: Bodart's printed commanders. Moriggl has Augereau, commandant of the VII Army Corps, arrive at Bregenz only at noon on 14 November, while the French General of Division Mathieu made the first offer and agreed the final terms at Dornbirn (claim side-a-command); Victoires has Augereau command the corps sent against the Vorarlberg, and General of Division Maurice Mathieu and General-Major Wolfskehl settle the articles under authority from their generals-in-chief. Both accounts name Jellachich as side B's commander (claim side-b-command). English rendering (ours): as in claim bodart-strength.

entries.claim_value: Krauss estimates that at least 18,000-20,000 infantry and about 2,000-3,000 horse of side B (Austrian) may have taken part in the action at Haslach, and says the Austrian regiments entered the fight one after another.
entries.author_rationale: Krauss's estimate ('mochten ... teilgenommen haben'), read from the page image; no return or basis is named in the passages read. It is separate from Bodart's 25,000 (claim bodart-strength) and from Dupont's figures (claim french-figures-for-side-b), and its parts are not added here. English renderings (ours): 'at least 18,000-20,000 infantry and about 2000-3000 horse may have taken part on the Austrian side in the action at Haslach'; 'had the result that the Austrian regiments entered the fight one after another'.

No passage read gives a loss for side A, and Bodart prints none. Grouchy describes a most murderous crossfire from the Prussian infantry and the breaking of the gates under Prussian fire, but gives no figure. No loss is stated, so it is left unknown, not set to zero.

entries.claim_value: Side A (French), its own account in Koch: in execution of the orders the marshal gave after settling at Cosenza on 15 December the final dispositions for the attack, a corps of 1,200 men under Colonel Huard, acting as general of brigade, invested the fortress on the 18th; Verdier set out on the 22nd with 2,500 men and 6 pieces of ordnance and was followed the next day by a column of 1,000 men brought by General Reynier. Before Bodart's dates, Verdier had left Cosenza on 3 December for the first attempt with 1,300 men, 2 howitzers and 2 mountain pieces.
entries.author_rationale: Side A's history, read from the page images. Koch's three bodies make 4,700 (our arithmetic), Bodart's figure (claim bodart-strength); the passages read give no single strength for the force before the place on one day and no count of its losses or reinforcements during the siege. Koch gives the day of the investment as 'the 18th' without a month, in a narrative that has just brought the marshal to Cosenza on 15 December; read as 18 December, it is Bodart's first date. The page image of p. 282 is heavily inked, and the transcription reads the first figure of '22' by its shape. Koch's 'his orders' follow the marshal's instructions to Reynier, and the force moved in execution of them, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): 'meanwhile it had to be finished: the marshal went on 15 December to Cosenza, where he settled the final dispositions concerning the attack on Amantea' (p. 281); 'in execution of his orders, a corps of 1,200 men led by Colonel Huard, performing the' (p. 281) 'functions of general of brigade, formed the investment of the fortress on the 18th. Verdier set out on the 22nd with 2,500 men and 6 pieces of ordnance; he was followed the next day by a column of 1,000 men brought by General Reynier, who directed all the operations of the siege' (p. 282); 'reassured on this point, Verdier, in accordance with the marshal's orders, left Cosenza on 3 December to reduce Amantea, at the head of 1,300 men, 2 howitzers and 2 mountain pieces' (p. 280).

entries.claim_value: Bodart names General of Division Savary as side A's (French) commander and Major General v. Lecoq as side B's (Prussian). Höpfner: Major General and Engineer Brigadier Schöler was appointed commandant of Hameln in May, and Lecoq commanded his own corps, which reached 4000 men on 23 October and camped at the foot of the Klütberg from the 24th; at the Wehrberg Warte Lecoq drafted the capitulation and the commandant signed it, and Schöler refused to let Colonel Caprivi sign as well, since he, the general, was commandant of the town and of the forts. Savary announced his arrival as commander of the besieging corps on the evening of the 19th, sent by Napoleon's order of 18 November to take command of the blockading troops; the 32nd Bulletin, of 16 November, already says that he had been charged with the blockade of Hameln with the Dutch division.
entries.author_rationale: Bodart's printed commanders, read from the frame transcription, with Höpfner and the 32nd Bulletin, read from the page images. Bodart's choice of Lecoq rather than the commandant is kept as printed; the capitulation's text, which would show who signed it, was not seen. The Bulletin is dated two days before the order of 18 November as Höpfner gives it; both are kept (claim side-a-command). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; 'immediately after the taking of possession Major General Strachwitz commanded in Hameln, but in May Major General and Engineer Brigadier Schöler, an old man of 75, physically and mentally wholly dulled, and therefore slow to decide and extremely anxious, was appointed commandant'; 'this was the state of things when General Hagken's detachment was drawn into the garrison on 23 October, and in exchange the 1st battalion of Oranien, 810 men strong, joined General Lecoq, whose corps thereby reached a strength of 4000 men'; 'on 24 October General Lecoq led his corps into a camp at the foot of the Klütberg, and had its entrenchment begun at once'; 'General Savary now wanted to dictate the points of capitulation at once, but General Lecoq declined this, drafted the capitulation in French himself, and the commandant signed the collated copy after General Lecoq had assured him that there was nothing more to object to'; 'the colonel answered only with tears. When General Savary asked him to sign the capitulation as well, General Schöler refused this with the remark that the colonel did not need to sign, since he, the general, was commandant of the town and of the forts'; 'quite unexpectedly a parlementaire was again announced on the evening of the 19th'; 'it was Captain Charles with a letter from General Savary, in which he announced to the commandant his arrival as commander of the besieging corps, and at the same time expressed his pleasure at the commandant's sensible views of the state of affairs, adding that he nevertheless could not accept the conditions put, since the King of Prussia had not a battalion left and was himself in flight; he wished to settle the rest orally, and left it to them to fix the time and place for it'; 'under 18 November Napoleon at last directed General Savary from Berlin to leave at once and go before Hameln to take command of the blockading troops; the guns from Rinteln were to bombard the place and so hasten its surrender, the field guns to defend the entrenchments; the 12th light infantry regiment was already on its way from Kassel as reinforcement; the commandant there, General Lagrange, was further to be asked to send off some cavalry; the garrison of Hameln could be granted a capitulation by which it would be prisoners of war, the officers released on parole, but the private soldiers transported to France etc.'; '32nd Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 16 November 1806'; 'General Savary has been charged with the blockade of Hameln with the Dutch division'.

entries.claim_value: The passages read place side B's rearguard on the road short of Parsdorf and its army in line on the height of Anzing, and side A's cavalry on the road from Munich; Munich had been evacuated. They name no works from which either side fought.
entries.author_rationale: none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed. English renderings as in claims side-b-engaged and side-a-information.

No passage read says what side B knew of side A's strength, approaches or mine during the siege of 18 December to 6 February. The alarm Colletta describes, raised by a child on a December night, belongs to the first attempt, before Bodart's dates (claim side-a-command). Unknown.

No passage read gives side A's loss in men, and Bodart prints none. Schönhals has one French light battalion lay down its arms near Neuhaus without the Austrians being able to carry the prisoners off (claim side-b-command), and Alombert and Colin call the first fight a short and bloody mêlée (OCR; claim side-a-command). Unknown, not zero.

entries.claim_value: Bodart places Groß-Glogau, a town in Prussia, province of Silesia, on the Oder, 50 km north of Liegnitz; the 30th Bulletin calls Glogau the capital of Upper Silesia. Höpfner: the fortress lay on both banks of the Oder, with its main wall on the left bank, the Dom-Retranchement on the right bank and the Sternschanze at its upper junction with the Oder; the Schießhaus, a farmstead, stood close below the town on the Oder; side A approached especially along the avenue of Rauschwitz; the batteries on the right bank stood behind the dam before Zerbau; a bridge at Beichau was to keep the connection between the banks; and on 30 November the roads were so bad from the wet weather that the small mortars and the howitzers, brought up on sledges, could be put into the batteries only at 8 in the evening.
entries.author_rationale: Location and works as described, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription). Höpfner's Plan Nr. XVII of Glogau was not inspected, and where each work stood is taken only from the descriptions; the works themselves are in claim fortification. The 30th Bulletin's 'capital of Upper Silesia' is kept as printed. The ground is tagged inherited; the weather and the roads are kept with it. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(town in Prussia, province of Silesia, on the Oder, 50 km north of Liegnitz)'; '30th Bulletin of the Grande Armée. Berlin, 10 November 1806'; 'Prince Jérôme has had the place of Glogau, capital of Upper Silesia, blockaded by Brigade General Lefebvre at the head of 2,000 Bavarian horse. The place was bombarded on the 8th by 10 howitzers served by light artillery. The Prince has praised the conduct of the Bavarian cavalry. General Deroy, with his division, invested Glogau on the 9th; talks have been opened for its surrender'; 'the most reliable battalion of the garrison, the battalion von Grevenitz, occupied the weakest places of the main wall on the left bank of the Oder, the less reliable battalion von Tschepe the rest of it, and the worst battalion, von Zastrow, the Dom-Retranchement [the cathedral entrenchment] on the right bank of the Oder; a detachment of the best invalids held the Sternschanze [star fort] at the fortress's upper junction with the Oder, the rest of the invalids occupied the gorge' (the sentence continues on p. 19); 'of this work; the cavalry and the Jäger were used to patrol the abandoned outworks. The burghers did duty in the town' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 18); 'during this cannonade the enemy set fire in several places to the stock of wood of 10-15,000 Klafter [cords] standing by the Schießhaus [shooting house], a farmstead close below the town on the Oder'; 'at last on 22 November, when the enemy had approached with his pits especially along the avenue of Rauschwitz, Lieutenant Sommerfeld was sent forward with the detachment of the regiment Zenge into the nearest outworks, and on the proposal of the place's engineer a 12-pounder was brought into the counterguard of the Prussian ravelin, so as to take the' (the sentence continues on p. 27); 'battery received only 2 cannon and 1 howitzer. On the right bank only ½ a Bavarian battery and a Württemberg battery brought up, or 9 guns, had been placed behind the dam to the left before Zerbau' (the first sentence ends the sentence begun on p. 20); 'on 17 November early the Bavarians set fire to the wood still standing at the Schießhaus, whereby the building itself was laid in ashes. The Württembergers relieved the brigade Siebein on this day, which moved to the left bank; a bridge at Beichau was to maintain the connection between the two banks'; 'on the evening of the same day six vessels with siege guns and munition arrived at Beichau. On 29 November the unloading of the projectiles began, which were housed in the church of Prostau; on the 30th the guns, 6 small and 4 heavy mortars and 4 howitzers of heavy calibre, were disembarked, but the roads had become so bad from the wet weather that had set in that only in the evening at 8 o'clock could the small mortars and the howitzers, brought up on sledges, be put into the batteries, and, together with the field howitzers already standing there, the following distribution took place: in battery No. 1, 2 mortars and 2 howitzers; in No. 2, 3 and 5, 2 howitzers each; in No. 4 and 6, 2 mortars and 2 howitzers each'.

entries.claim_value: Side A in its own reports: Bernadotte had with him only 12 guns and 12 caissons for his whole corps, the rest having stayed behind at the defile of Dornburg. His order gave the attack on the first bridge to the 32e and a battalion of the 9e léger, seconded by 3 pieces of light artillery; once master of the town he sent the 96e to support the 9e and 32e, and immediately afterwards passed the 2e and 4e hussars and all Rivaud's division but a reserve battalion; the 2 divisions and the 2 hussar regiments moved on the enemy. When a column showed itself on his rear on the left bank of the Saale, Drouet's division, already recalled, arrived faster than expected, and Bernadotte ordered Drouet to have the column attacked by the 27e léger and the 95e; he had also brought up the 94e to support the great attack. Höpfner has Bernadotte order Düpont to attack with the 4 battalions of the 9th light and 32nd line regiments and keep the 2 battalions of the 96th and the hussars in reserve at Passendorf. Dupont wrote that his guns were few.
entries.author_rationale: Units from Bernadotte's and Dupont's letters and Höpfner, read from the page images; no source read gives a headcount for side A other than Höpfner's and Bodart's 16,000 (claims hoepfner-strength, bodart-strength). English renderings (ours): Bernadotte, 'it is well to observe to Your Majesty that I had with me only 12 guns and 12 caissons for my whole army corps, the rest having stayed behind at the defile of Dornburg'; as in claim foucart-side-b for the first attack and the 96th; 'immediately afterwards I passed the 2nd and 4th hussars and the whole division Rivaud, except for one reserve battalion'; 'the 2 divisions and the 2 hussar regiments moved on the enemy'; as in claim side-a-information for the column on the left bank; 'I had already recalled the division Drouet; this general, at the sound of the guns, had so pressed his march that he arrived much faster than could have been expected'; 'I ordered him to have the column that had appeared on our left and behind our line attacked by the 27th light and the 95th'; 'I had brought up the 94th to support the great attack'; Höpfner, 'but now Marshal Bernadotte ordered General Düpont to undertake the attack with the 4 battalions of the 9th light and the 32nd line regiments, and to leave the 2 battalions of the 96th line regiment and the hussars at Passendorf in reserve'; Dupont, 'while the enemy played his artillery on us, to which we could reply only weakly, given the small number of our guns'.

entries.claim_value: Side B (Austrian), side A's figures: Dupont's division journal says General Werneck capitulated with his army corps, 6,000 infantry, 800 cavalry, 25 guns and 3 generals strong.
entries.author_rationale: Side A's figure, read from the page image; the journal does not say how it was obtained, and it differs from Werneck's own statement and from Bodart's figure. The cavalry reserve's totals for the whole day are in claim side-b-losses-reported. English rendering (ours): 'General Werneck capitulates with his army corps, 6,000 men of infantry, 800 men of cavalry, 25 guns and 3 generals strong'.

entries.claim_value: The Emperor, going to Munich, put Ney under Murat but had him first take Ulm, writing to him directly: 'surround Ulm in the course of tomorrow'; the dragoons on foot stayed under Ney's orders. Ney left Dupont two squadrons of the 1st hussars and two dragoon regiments of Bourcier's division, and sent his orders for the 11th late on the evening of the 10th: the 1st division under General Dupont was to blockade Ulm on the left bank of the Danube. His instruction told Dupont to close in on Ulm as far as he could and summon its commandant, to push his right to the Blau, to occupy the wooded heights behind Haslacherhof and to agree with General Baraguey d'Hilliers on placing the dragoons on foot, who were to support his division and form its reserve; he was to avoid compromising his division against superior forces or splitting it too much, and to keep his posts well entrenched and covered by abatis. On the morning of the 11th a third instruction told him to get ladders and tackle to scale Ulm's walls. Dupont replied that he was marching at once on Ulm.
entries.author_rationale: The chain from the Emperor through Ney to Dupont, from the orders printed by the French official history (OCR) and Krauss's summary of the same instruction. The orders set the investment; the decision to fight at Haslach was Dupont's (claim side-a-decision). English renderings (ours): 'Ney will be under Murat's orders, but he will begin by taking Ulm, and the Emperor gives him orders directly for this operation'; 'as the Emperor is going to Munich'; 'surround Ulm in the course of tomorrow'; 'the dragoons on foot will continue to remain under your orders'; 'I leave him two squadrons of the 1st hussars and two regiments of dragoons of General Bourcier's division'; 'Marshal Ney sends his orders for the 11th at a late hour of the evening of the 10th'; 'the 1st division, under the orders of General Dupont, will blockade Ulm on the left bank of the Danube'; 'you will please, my dear General, close in on the place of Ulm as much as you can, and make a summons to the commandant'; 'it is very important that you push your right tomorrow as far as the Blau, where it will be supported'; 'you will occupy the wooded heights behind Haslacherhof'; 'who are to support your division and form its reserve'; 'you must avoid, my dear General, compromising your division against superior forces and splitting it up too much'; 'your posts well entrenched and covered with abatis'; 'on the morning of the 11th a third instruction was sent to General Dupont'; 'all the tackle needed to scale the walls of Ulm'; Dupont, 'I am marching at once to move on Ulm'; Krauss, 'Dupont was to avoid playing his division against superior forces'.

entries.claim_value: Bodart calls Breslau the capital of Prussian Silesia. Höpfner: the works were extensive and partly hard to connect, and the fortress was divided into 4 main fronts; the main wall was surrounded by wide water ditches, with outworks including the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork, the Ohlau ravelin, the ravelin R. before the Ziegel gate, the Dom and the Springstern, and an enveloppe around the fortress; the Bürgerwerder, whose works were held as an outpost, was separated from side A's approaches by an arm of the Oder; the Oder bank where side A's left parallel rested lay 10-12 feet above the water, with a sandbank reachable unseen from the Bürgerwerder; and the extensive suburbs, which hindered the defence and were not cleared, gave side A's skirmishers cover until the garrison burnt the Nikolai, Hinter-Dom and Ohlau suburbs and the nearest houses of the Oder suburb. Blein found the main wall unrevetted at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates, the wet main ditch over 120 feet wide, an earthen enveloppe with lunettes at its salients, and the outer ditch around it 60-70 feet wide and 6-7 feet deep. In Vandamme's expectation, as Höpfner gives it, a population of 60,000 would not be sacrificed to works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. Foucart places Höflchen, Montbrun's first position, a league from the town, and Gnichwitz 20 km from Breslau on the road to Schweidnitz. Höpfner has frost set in at 3 in the afternoon of a day before 2 January, open water being the fortress's only protection against a coup de main given the unreliability and weakness of the garrison, and, after the night to the 3rd, the weather turn milder again and the water stay open.
entries.author_rationale: Location, works and weather as described, read from the page images (Bodart's from the frame transcription). Höpfner's Plan XVIII of Breslau was not inspected, and where each work stood is taken only from the descriptions; the works' state and occupation are in claim fortification. Blein's findings are Höpfner's report of his reconnaissance. The ground is tagged inherited; the weather is kept with it. The day the frost set in is dated on p. 108, which was read in the OCR only and not registered. Foucart prints 'Schweibnitz' on p. 95 and 'Schweidnitz' on p. 97; the renderings keep his spelling. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '(capital of Prussian Silesia)'; 'because of the extent of the works and their partly difficult connection with one another, the fortress was divided into 4 main fronts, and each was entrusted to a staff officer of the infantry as divisional commander and an older artillery officer, for the complete equipment of the works and their eventual defence'; 'it was thus the government's intention to hold and defend all the outworks, but when General Lindener arrived on 6 November he brought it about that this plan was abandoned and the defence restricted to the main wall, surrounded by wide water ditches; only the Nikolai crownwork, the Mühlberg redoubt, the Oder crownwork,' (the sentence continues on p. 48); 'the Ohlau ravelin and the ravelin R. before the Ziegel gate1) were to remain occupied, while the guns of the other outworks were to be brought back to the main wall' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 47; the note refers to Höpfner's plan XVIII of Breslau); 'only later, when the garrison had received some reinforcement, were the important and already palisaded outworks, the Dom and the Springstern, also drawn into the defence'; 'the enveloppe that surrounded the fortress was to be occupied only by day, by single marksmen and Jäger'; 'considering that the Bavarian advance guard enclosed the fortress on the right bank of the Oder too on the 8th, so that the use of the horse artillery on that bank was much restricted, while the Bürgerwerder was threatened by the enemy's works in the night to the 8th, the governor ordered Lieutenant Fiebig to move with the horse artillery into the works on the Bürgerwerder and take over their defence. La-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 54); 'ter these works were gradually also occupied by infantry, 8 heavy guns and some cavalry. The intention was to keep the Bürgerwerder occupied, as an outpost against the enemy's works, for as long as the enemy would allow it from the right side of the Oder, where the work covering the Werder had been left unoccupied' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 53); 'from the left second parallel an approach trench with a small place of arms was to be pushed forward, so that from it the Württemberg Jäger could harass the Prussian gunners on the Bürgerwerder; but in the night to the 14th they struck quite unexpectedly on the arm of the Oder that separated the enemy from the works of the Bürgerwerder'; 'since the bank of the Oder where the first-named parallel rested lay 10-12 feet above the water level, and from the parallel one could reach a sandbank lying there unseen from the Bürgerwerder, this junction gave the besieger great advantages'; 'the clearing of the suburbs, which hindered a vigorous defence, was not done, partly in the hope of a relief by the Russian operations, partly because the government feared the mood of the numerous burghers if it destroyed these extensive buildings before the enemy forced it to, and partly, finally, because it was believed that when the enemy actually appeared it would still be possible to shoot them down and burn them'; 'since the enemy's tirailleurs lodged themselves in the houses of the Nikolai suburb and of the Schweidnitz Anger and harassed the foremost palisade tambours and even the communication between the Nikolai gate and the Scheeren bastion lying below it, the Nikolai suburb was set on fire in the evening at 6 o'clock.1)'; 'on 8 December and in the night to the 9th the defender also set fire to the nearest houses of the Oder suburb, to give the artillery of the Bürgerwerder and of the Oder crownwork a free view'; 'the garrison's artillery fired without pause on these works and set fire to the Hinter-Dom suburb, so as to be able to counter the enemy's batteries on the right bank and take from the enemy's tirailleurs the cover from which they could do harm to the troops on the low walls of the Dom'; 'in the evening the garrison had to set fire to the Ohlau suburb as well'; 'for want of a good plan of Breslau, already on 17, 18 and 19 December the engineer Colonel' (the sentence continues on p. 63); 'Blein had reconnoitred the works on the left bank of the Oder as thoroughly as possible and in doing so established that the main wall was not revetted at two extended places, namely at the Schweidnitz and Ohlau gates; that before the wet main ditch, over 120 feet wide, there was an enveloppe of earth, covered at its salient angles by lunettes with retired flanks; that these works were indeed provided with storm-poles and palisades, but were occupied only before the revetted front of the Nikolai gate, against which the siege works had so far been directed; and finally that the outer ditch surrounding the enveloppe had a width of 60-70 feet and a depth of 6-7 feet' (the end of the sentence begun on p. 62); 'on General Minucci's return, General Vandamme, who had ordered the building of 4 new batteries in order to bring into them a further 8 24-pounders, 6 12-pounders and 2 mortars that were arriving from Glogau, believed he must set the town seriously on fire and inform the governor of the defeat of the relief troops and of the means he possessed to destroy the town. He expected that a population of 60,000 inhabitants would not be sacrificed to the holding of works that owed their preservation only to the mild weather. All this was done without the knowledge of General Hédouville, although this general, as mentioned, was to continue the command in Jerome's name'; 'General Montbrun, preceding the Württemberg division, moved before Breslau by the left bank of the Oder. On the morning of the 6th he was a league from the town, at Höflchen, where he took position; he at once sent a party over to the right bank of the Oder to gather information on the arrival of the Bavarian troops, sent a detachment of 25 men and an officer to take post at Gnichwitz, 20 km from Breslau on the road to Schweibnitz, and dispatched to Schweibnitz a trusted man he had with him, with the task of reporting to him within two days the composition of the garrison of that place'; 'at 3 in the afternoon the sky cleared and it began to freeze. That was the most unfavourable thing that could befall the garrison; for only by open water was the fortress, given the unreliability and weakness of the garrison, secured against a coup de main. The necessary measures were taken for breaking the ice of the Oder and the fortress ditches'; 'on 2 January at 11 o'clock Colonel Duveyrier and Captain Hammerer were let in. Their business consisted in the request for the release of several persons, mostly of the female sex, and besides in the enumeration, repeated to weariness, of all the reasons that were to make the sur-' (the word and sentence continue on p. 110); 'render of the fortress necessary. Both officers were dismissed with expressions of courtesy, and at 3 o'clock the garrison's fire began again, at 5 o'clock a 2-hour bombardment by the enemy' (the first word ends the one begun on p. 109); 'in the night to the 3rd the enemy bombarded from 11 until 4 o'clock'; 'the weather turned milder again; the water stayed open'.

entries.claim_value: Bodart gives side A (French) as 6,000 men under General of Division Savary, and side B (Prussian) as the garrison of 3,000 men with 51 guns under Major General v. Strachwitz, which the French forced to capitulate without a stroke of the sword, after which the garrison fell into captivity as prisoners of war. By his stated rule his figures are the forces available for the engagement, rounded up.
entries.author_rationale: Bodart's printed entry, read from the page image in the frame transcription; one claim among several. Höpfner gives the garrison's parts and total (claim side-b-strength), the Emperor and Mortier other estimates (claim side-b-strength-french), and Höpfner and the French letters side A's troops (claim side-a-strength). Bodart's 3,000 is Höpfner's 2911 rounded up, and his 51 guns are Höpfner's 39 cannon, 10 howitzers and 2 mortars, without the 12 Wallbüchsen (our comparison and arithmetic). His 6,000 for side A is the figure he prints for Savary's force at Hameln (B376d; our comparison); no passage read gives a total for side A at Nienburg. Which source Bodart used was not checked. English rendering (ours) of Bodart's rules: p. 46, 'the strengths given are always those forces that were disposable for the battle'; p. 47, 'the strength and loss figures were rounded up by the author'. English rendering (ours) of the heading and entry: '1806 26/11. capitulation of Nienburg'; 'the French (6,000 men) under General of Division Savary force the Prussian garrison (3,000 men, 51 guns) under Major General v. Strachwitz to capitulate without a stroke of the sword, after which the garrison fell into captivity as prisoners of war'.

entries.claim_value: Pultusk is a town in Russian Poland on the right bank of the Narew, 50 km north of Warsaw (Bodart). In Höpfner the battlefield is bounded on the east by the Narew and on the south and south-west by woods, rises gently northward from them and falls again toward Pultusk, so that a gently rising but fairly extended height hides a position at Pultusk from an enemy coming out of the woods; in the thaw the rich loam had dissolved into a pulp that hindered every arm, and guns could be moved only with the utmost exertion; the approach through the woods bounding the field on the west seems to have been particularly difficult. The Russian left leaned on Pultusk and the right on the wood of Mosino; General Baggowut stood on the road to Warsaw beyond a ravine running down to the Narew; the Mosino brook, in that season, did not allow a wider turning movement, so the wood had to be taken; and woods a few thousand paces off in front hid the enemy's strength. Lannes found the enemy established on the plain before the town, his right resting on a bridge at the far end of the town and his left on another bridge at its entrance; his men fought in mud to mid-thigh, the wind and hail knocked them over, and all his artillery stuck in the marshes. In the 3rd corps's journal the thaw had been complete for two days, rare in Poland in that season; the ground was clayey and marshy and the roads frightful, two hours being needed for a short league; the enemy was formed on the plateau of Pultusk, his right, bent back at a right angle, crowning the heights over Moszyn; and that part of his line would have been thrown into the ravine of Bialowizna but for a strong reserve posted in a thicket parallel to the road. The journal of the 5th dragoon division, quoted by the editor, has marshy ground where the horses sank in the mud to their bellies and shifting, very muddy ground before the town. On 28 December Lannes wrote that one could not take a step without sinking into the mud to mid-thigh; the editor's note and Corbineau give the Narew as 25 to 30 toises wide at Pultusk.
entries.author_rationale: Bodart's location line, read from the page image in the frame transcription; Höpfner and Foucart from the page images (Höpfner pp. 109-112; Foucart pp. 462-464, 466-469, 514, 515 and 517). The ground and the weather were given, so the claim is tagged inherited; the choice of the position was Bennigsen's (claim side-b-command). Lannes's two bridges are not reconciled with Höpfner's wings, which rest on the town and the Mosino wood (our comparison). The dragoon journal's first paragraph is dated 'Le 22' as printed, though its note mark is set in Lannes's account of the 26th; the figure is not corrected. Höpfner's plan of the battle was not inspected. English renderings (ours): Bodart, '1806 26/12. Battle at Pultusk (4.)'; 'victory of the French (24 battalions, 27 squadrons, 55 guns = 26,000 men) under Marshal Lannes over the Russians (66 battalions, 75 squadrons, 200 guns = 44,000 men) under General of Cavalry von Bennigsen'; '(town in Russian Poland, on the right bank of the Narew, 50 km north of Warsaw)'; Höpfner, 'the battlefield at Pultusk is bounded on the east by the Narew, on the south and south-west by woods, rises gently from these woods toward the north and falls again toward Pultusk, so that from an enemy debouching from these woods a position at Pultusk is hidden by a gently rising but fairly extended height'; 'but at the time of the battle, the thaw having set in, the rich loam soil had dissolved into a pulp, so that every arm found an obstacle in it, and the movement of the guns could be accomplished only with the utmost exertion'; 'an approach to the Russian position through the woods that bound the battlefield on the west seems to have been particularly difficult'; 'the left wing leaned on Pultusk, the right wing on the wood of Mosino'; 'on the road to Warsaw and beyond a ravine that runs down toward the Narew'; 'as the state of the Mosino brook in that season did not well allow a wider turning movement, so that the enemy necessarily had to take that wood to advance further'; 'the flaw of the position at Pultusk, that it was surrounded in front, at a few thousand paces' distance, by wood that hid the enemy's strength and dispositions'; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 27 December 1806'; 'I found the enemy established on the plain before this town; his advance guard' (p. 462); 'the enemy fell back on his main body, which had its right resting on the bridge at the far end of the town, and its left on another bridge at the entrance of the town'; 'we fought from 10 in the morning until 6 in the evening in mud up to mid-thigh'; 'Your Majesty saw the weather of the day; the wind and the hail knocked our soldiers over'; 'all our artillery had stuck in the marshes, and despite all General Foucher's efforts it could hardly serve us and it is at this moment in bad condition...'; the journal, 'here are the operations of the 3rd division of the 3rd corps during the day of the 26th'; '(extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd corps)'; 'the thaw had been complete for two days, which in this season is rare in Poland'; 'the ground the army was crossing was clayey and marshy; the roads were frightful... Two hours were needed to cover a short league'; 'the enemy was formed on the plateau of Pultusk, on which he rested his left, and his right, bending back at a right angle, crowned the heights that overhang Moszyn'; 'this part of the enemy line would have been entirely thrown into the ravine of Bialowizna but for the help of a strong reserve which, placed in a thicket parallel to the road, stopped our first echelons'; the dragoon journal, 'on the 22nd, as soon as the 5th corps could defile at 10 in the morning, the division moved into the position it had occupied the day before'; 'the 1st brigade, General Boussart, directed to the left, followed the movements of the division Suchet in marshy ground where the horses sank in the mud up to their bellies, and so intimidated the enemy that he did not dare to undertake a charge'; 'the 2nd brigade, General Viallannes, stayed alone facing the town, occupying the centre of the army corps on shifting and very muddy ground, manoeuvring under the enemy's guns and opposing every attempt at this point'; '(journal of march of the 5th dragoon division)'; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'it is impossible to form an idea of the country; one cannot take a step without sinking into the mud up to mid-thigh'; the editor, 'the Narew is 25 to 30 toises wide at Pultusk'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'the width of the river is 25 to 30 toises'.

entries.claim_value: Side B (Prussian) in Höpfner: the garrison consisted of the 3rd musketeer battalions of the regiments Kunheim, Arnim, Möllendorf, Larisch, Winning, Braunschweig-Oels and Pirch and a fortress artillery company, or 100 officers and 5184 men, whose good will made the bravest resistance possible. It could have been much increased by taking in the officers, NCOs and men passing through in large numbers and arming them with the muskets sent from Berlin to Stettin in two barges, and its total want of cavalry could have been remedied; but the governor kept back no man for fortress duty. The fortress had 187 fully serviceable guns and 94 still usable in an emergency, of which 100 of various calibres were already mounted on the ramparts and the most important points of defence when the French arrived.
entries.author_rationale: Side B's history, read from the page image of p. 217. The garrison and guns were the place's own before the French arrived, so the claim is tagged inherited. Höpfner's officers and men total 5284 and his guns 281 (our arithmetic). English renderings (ours): 'the garrison consisted of the 3rd musketeer battalions of the regiments Kunheim, Arnim, Möllendorf, Larisch, Winning, Braunschweig-Oels and Pirch and a fortress artillery company, or of 100 officers 5184 men, whose good will made the bravest resistance possible'; 'this garrison could have been very considerably increased if the officers, NCOs and privates passing through in great numbers had been taken in and armed with the muskets sent from Berlin to Stettin in two barges; likewise the total lack of cavalry could have been fully remedied'; 'but the governor saw fit not only to keep back no man for fortress duty, but he even refused General Bila II passage and thereby caused the capitulation of Anklam, as will be shown later'; 'in guns the fortress had 187 fully serviceable pieces and 94 still usable in an emergency, of which, at the time of the French arrival, 100 pieces of various calibres were already set up on the ramparts and the most important points of defence'.

entries.claim_value: Side B held the citadel of Spandau, a permanent fortress that Lannes describes as standing in the middle of a lake and capable of a great defence. Höpfner says the citadel was in no particular state but had no practicable breach, nor could one easily be made, because its rampart consisted of several tiers of vaults; even an enemy who approached it and seized the covered way could not cross the main ditch except under the fire of the works; but for want of time the parapets could not be raised, and gabions had to be made instead. Bertrand reported an enclosure with a parapet and about a dozen guns in battery around the fort, which seemed to him crowded with buildings and easy to set on fire.
entries.author_rationale: Coded B_fortified: the citadel's works were permanent and held by side B, so the claim is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'only on the 23rd did workers arrive from the country, who were now used to repair the citadel. It was in no particular condition, but there was also no practicable breach, nor could one easily be made, as the rampart consisted of several vaults lying one above the other'; 'but even if the enemy approached the citadel by means of it and seized the covered way, he was still not able to cross the main ditch except under the fire of the works' (OCR); 'it was just as disadvantageous that, likewise for want of time, no work could be done on raising the parapets; gabions had to be made instead' (OCR); Bertrand, as in claim side-b-strength-french for the heading and signature and in claim side-a-information for the enclosure (OCR); 'around the fort a dozen guns in battery' (OCR); 'the fort seems to me crowded with buildings and easy to set on fire' (OCR); Lannes, as in claim side-b-strength-french for the heading and date and in claim spandau-ground for the lake.

entries.claim_value: No passage read has either side fight from works. Side B stood before the town of Saalfeld, between the town and the Rabenstein with guns on a gentle rise, and in a line deployed with the Saale at its back (on a raised ridge commanding the valley, in M. de Mumpfling's report); side A had to debouch from the mountains before the prince's front and, in Mumpfling's report, held villages in low ground (OCR except the position at the Rabenstein). Two passages name works without showing anyone fighting from them: jäger and fusiliers driven back to the town took the covered way along its ditch and barricaded its gates in haste, while others still held before the town or withdrew fighting; and Höpfner's judgment that the jäger and fusiliers could have held the town, which had a wall and ditch, while the rest crossed the Saale describes a defence that was not made (OCR). Trees, bushes, garden walls and earth banks gave the French skirmishers cover (OCR).
entries.author_rationale: Code none_named: the places held were the approaches to the town, a ridge, a suburb, villages and mountain slopes, held without named works, and the garden walls covered skirmishers as ground, not as works. The barricaded gates and the town's wall are named, but no passage read has side B fight from them: the gates were barricaded in haste by troops already driven back, and Höpfner names the wall and ditch in his judgment of what the prince could have done. A coding that counted the barricaded gates would give B_fortified, and one that also counted the garden walls that covered the French skirmishers, both_fortified. The accounts agree on the code, so they are one claim, and a none_named code takes the phase unresolved; none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, as in claim hoepfner-side-b for the position at the Rabenstein (p. 268); as in claim saalfeld-ground for the deployment and the cover and in claim prince-decision for the position (OCR); 'in the long suburb at the gate of the town he already met part of the jäger and fusiliers, who had at last been driven back by the enemy advancing in superior force'; 'they had, leaving the town on the right, taken the covered way along the town ditch, and barricaded the town gates in haste'; 'some troops still held before the town or withdrew fighting'; 'the prince's jäger and fusiliers would have held the town, which had a wall and ditch, against the French advancing from Garnsdorf until the troops had reached their position on the right bank and the Saale bridge had been prepared for destruction or barricading' (OCR); Mumpfling, as in claim saalfeld-ground for the ridge and the villages (OCR).

No passage read gives a French loss at Ratkau or in the night surprise of Schwartau before it, and Bodart prints none. The corps capitulated without a fight on the morning of the 7th. No loss is stated, so it is left unknown, not set to zero.

entries.claim_value: The passages read name no works on either side in the fighting. Side B held the town, the Mosino wood and the ground beyond a ravine, with the main body's artillery in front of the first line at the most favourable points and a battery commanding the road to Strzegocin and Golymin (Höpfner); Lannes wrote that a formidable artillery the enemy had at the head of the bridge crushed his men whenever they advanced too far; and the 3rd corps's journal has a strong Russian reserve posted in a thicket parallel to the road. In Höpfner Bennigsen had a great battery set up on the flank of the French in the wood during the battle. Side A was ordered on 25 December to build a bridgehead once across the Narew; on 28 December, after the Russians had gone, Lannes held the left bank at the bridgehead with a company of grenadiers (Corbineau).
entries.author_rationale: Coded none_named: the cited passages describe where both sides stood and name no entrenchments, redoubts, abatis or other works used in the fighting. Lannes's 'à la tête du pont' places artillery at the end of the bridge without naming a work (our reading), and a battery or a thicket is not a work under the brief. The bridgehead of the order of 25 December was to be built after the crossing, and the one Corbineau names on the 28th was held after the battle. none_named reports the passages read, not proof that no works existed; Höpfner's plan of the battle was not inspected. English renderings (ours): Höpfner, 'the left wing leaned on Pultusk, the right wing on the wood of Mosino'; 'the artillery of the main body stood in front of the first line, placed at the most favourable points'; '2 battalions of the Tenginsk regiment stood in reserve; the 3rd battalion covered a battery that commanded the road to Strzegocin and Golymin; the Polish horse regiment stood between the wood and Mosino'; 'on the road to Warsaw and beyond a ravine that runs down toward the Narew'; 'General Bennigsen had a great battery [set up] on the right flank of the [French who had pushed forward] in the wood as far as the road from Strzegocin' (p. 116); '[the French who had] pushed forward [...] set up, and inflicted great losses on them' (p. 117); Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 27 December 1806'; 'the left withstood the fire of about 15,000 men, and but for a formidable artillery they had at the head of the bridge, whose fire crushed us when we advanced too far, this whole force would have been thrown into the river'; the journal, 'here are the operations of the 3rd division of the 3rd corps during the day of the 26th'; '(extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd corps)'; 'this part of the enemy line would have been entirely thrown into the ravine of Bialowizna but for the help of a strong reserve which, placed in a thicket parallel to the road, stopped our first echelons'; the major general, 'the major general to Marshal Lannes'; 'Slostowo, 25 December 1806'; 'the Emperor's intention, Marshal, is that you leave Nasielsk to make for Pultusk, cross the Narew there and build a bridgehead there at once'; Corbineau, 'General Corbineau to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 28 December 1806'; 'he has on the left bank, at the bridgehead, a company of grenadiers'.

entries.claim_value: Archduke Charles commanded side B. Koch says the offensive was forbidden him, so that he was to fight only for the security of his retreat, and that he chose the entrenched position of Caldiero to receive the battle. During the night after the fighting of the 29th he drew Wetzel's brigade, Vogelsang with the grenadier brigades of Lippa and Hohenlohe, and the regiments Archduke Charles uhlans and Savoy dragoons forward into the position for his attack, and his disposition sent Simbschen from Colognola alta against Lavagno, Bellegarde's 2nd column, under the Archduke's personal direction, along the chaussée against Vago, and Reuss and Nordmann against side A's right flank and rear. The very unfavourable weather made him hold back the middle columns; when he heard firing on his left he attacked, Bellegarde advancing along the chaussée against Strà. When side A's skirmishers followed his retreating infantry close up to the works, he had Vogelsang advance from the reserve with Lippa's grenadiers and the regiment Eszterházy and led them forward in person (Angeli; Koch has him put himself at the head of Vogelsang's grenadiers, supported by Esterhazy's regiment). He sent grenadier support to Colognola and ordered Bellegarde to go there, but Simbschen's dispositions had already largely averted the danger. When Lenchantin's brigade had pushed beyond Caldiero he launched Hohenlohe's grenadier brigade from the reserve behind the position, while Archduke Maximilian led the rallied battalions forward again. On the 31st, after Nordmann was badly wounded, Colloredo took command and brought up the reserves, and Reuss threw a regiment with several hundred Croats on Verdier's right flank and sent a strong column of Hungarian grenadiers toward Gombione (Koch). After Bubna brought the official news of the disaster at Ulm, the Archduke resolved to break free at any price and retreat, and so to attack side A's left the following day and force it into full retreat (Angeli).
entries.author_rationale: Side B's decisions from Angeli, written from the Archduke's relation and his generals' reports (source notes 63-65), and from Koch (page images except the passages marked OCR below; counts of battalions and squadrons seen only in the OCR are not restated). Koch's statement that the offensive was forbidden the Archduke concerns his orders from above, which were not read. English renderings (ours): Koch, 'Prince Charles for his part, to whom the offensive was forbidden, was to fight only for the security of his retreat and took his measures accordingly' (OCR); 'and chose, to receive the battle, the entrenched position of Caldiero, from which he hoped to crush with his centre the divisions that had forced the crossing in his presence' (OCR); Angeli, 'the brigade of GM Wetzel, which had already arrived in Villanova, was drawn forward into the position, and besides FML Vogelsang with the grenadier brigades of GM Lippa and GM Prince Hohenlohe (... (OCR) battalions), then the regiments Archduke Charles uhlans and Savoy dragoons (... (OCR) squadrons), was likewise directed there from S. Gregorio' (OCR); 'all these arrangements were carried out during the night' (OCR); 'Masséna's thrusts ripened in him ... the plan of attack, for whose sake the whole centre, except for a single (OCR) brigade, was taken forward into the position of Caldiero' (OCR); 'on the right wing FML Simbschen with the brigades of GM Soudain and Oberst Pfanzelter, then 4 squadrons of Kienmayer hussars, in all 10½ battalions, 4 squadrons, advances at daybreak from Colognola alta by Donzellino against Lavagno'; 'a 2nd column of 18 battalions, 14 squadrons, consisting of the brigades of GM Frimont, GM Wetzel and GM Mihaljevich, then 1 chevau-légers regiment and 2 squadrons of hussars, is assembled by General of Cavalry Count Bellegarde at Strà' (p. 115), 'from where it will advance under Archduke Charles's personal direction on the chaussée against Vago' (p. 116, OCR); 'on the left wing FML Prince Reuss marches with the brigade of GM Kalnássy and the uhlan regiment Archduke Charles in the night from S. Gregorio by Belfiore di Porcile to about the work at Chiavighette' (OCR) 'and advances by Gombioni against Calderino into the enemy's right flank' (OCR); 'and attacks, at the same time as FML Prince Reuss's column, the enemy standing at Sabionara and Lepio in flank and rear' (OCR); 'the highly unfavourable weather however put the whole undertaking so seriously in question that Archduke Charles did not let the two (OCR) middle columns advance' (OCR); 'no sooner had Archduke Charles noticed the firing on his left wing than he too went over to the attack' (OCR); 'just as Gardanne was about to advance astride the chaussée against Caldiero, General of Cavalry Bellegarde advanced with ... (OCR) battalions and the chevau-légers regiment Kaiser Franz in closed masses along the chaussée against Strà' (OCR); 'followed the scattered infantry in dense swarms close on their heels right up to the works, so that the guns of the position could no longer act' (OCR); 'he had FML Vogelsang advance from the reserve with the grenadier brigade of GM Lippa, then the infantry regiment Eszterházy no. ... (OCR), and led these ... (OCR) battalions with band playing in person against the enemy' (OCR); Koch, 'then the Archduke attempts a last effort; he puts himself at the head of Vogelsang's grenadiers, supported by the regiment of Esterhazy' (OCR); Angeli, 'he ordered 1 (OCR) grenadier battalion to Colognola in support and charged General of Cavalry Bellegarde to go there himself and to throw back the enemy at any price' (OCR); 'before this reinforcement reached its destination, however, the danger had for the most part already been averted by FML Simbschen's well-judged dispositions and the bravery of the troops' (OCR); 'when the brigade Lenchantin had already pushed on beyond Caldiero between the heights of S. Matia and Monte Zovo, he let the grenadier brigade of GM Prince Hohenlohe, still standing in reserve behind the position, break out' (OCR); 'meanwhile Archduke Maximilian rallied the battalions that had come back and likewise led them forward to a renewed attack' (OCR); 'GM Nordmann, whose example spurred the men to brave endurance, was badly wounded on the parapet. GM Colloredo now took over the command and exercised it with equal resolution' (OCR); Koch, 'but as the attack became more serious and the defenders of the work had difficulty holding it, General Colloredo took command and brought up the reserves'; 'on the other hand the Prince of Reuss, finding himself compromised, threw a regiment with several hundred Croats on Verdier's right flank and directed a strong column of Hungarian grenadiers on Gombione'; Angeli, 'in the night from the ... to the ... (OCR) GM Count Bubna had arrived from Vienna on the Emperor's commission and brought, among other things, the official news of the catastrophe at Ulm' (OCR); 'this was for Archduke Charles one reason more to break free from the enemy at any price and to begin the retreat in the best possible condition. From this arose the decision to attack the enemy the next day on his left wing and to force him into complete retreat' (OCR).

entries.claim_value: Side A attacked. Bodart has a victory of the French. In Höpfner, Lannes decided to attack the Russians; the French advanced parallel to the Russian front, and about 11 General Claparède began the attack on General Baggowut's detachment, while General Suchet attacked the Mosino wood with the 34th regiment; later General d'Aultanne attacked the Russian right flank with half battalions at 50 paces' interval, and the French right and centre went to the attack again. Lannes reported that as soon as he was formed he had the enemy's advance guard attacked, then ordered the left bridge attacked and sent troops against the right bridge; the 3rd corps's journal has the 3rd division attack the enemy's flank by half battalions and echelons at 50 paces. Side B defended its position.
