Its charges and counterattacks were made within it: General Koschin's attack on Wedell's flank, Barclay's renewed attack, Baggowut's recrossing of the ravine and Somow's bayonet attack (Höpfner); and Lannes reported that the enemy sent about 8,000 infantry and 3 cavalry regiments against his right to outflank him, and later a column from his right to try again. In Höpfner the Russians only beat off the French attacks and nowhere made a counterstroke, and 29 Russian battalions never came into action.
entries.author_rationale: Coded A_attacked: side A attacked side B's position at Pultusk; side B's charges and counterattacks were made within its own defended position, which by the brief do not make the defender an attacker, and Höpfner says the Russians nowhere made a counterstroke. Lannes, side A's commander at this engagement (Bodart), decided the attack on the field (claim lannes-decision), so the claim is tagged commander_created; the order to take Pultusk came from above (claim side-a-objectives), and the 3rd division's attack was its own general's decision (claim daultanne-decision). English renderings (ours): Bodart, as in claim bodart-strength; Höpfner, 'however, the French marshals were too used to the most exact obedience to their Emperor's orders for Marshal Lannes to have long doubted what was to be done in this case; he decided to attack the Russians'; 'in this formation, with a strengthened right wing, the French advanced parallel to the Russian front, and about 11 o'clock General Claparède began the attack on General Baggowut's detachment'; 'during this fight on the Russian left wing, General Suchet with the infantry of the left wing had turned against General Barclay de Tolly, pushed forward a swarm of skirmishers and attacked the Mosino wood with the 34th Regiment'; 'with half battalions, 50 paces' interval between them, General d'Aultanne at once went to the attack in thick driving snow'; 'during this victorious fight in the Mosino wood the French had set up the artillery they had brought on the height the Russian cavalry had left, fired on General Baggowut's detachment in its right flank, and had then gone to the attack again with the right wing and the centre, together with the second line'; 'General Koschin seized the moment when General Wedell offered him his left flank and was at the same time attacked in front by 1 battalion of the Starokol Regiment and 1 Jäger battalion, and threw himself on his flank'; 'General Barclay, so considerably reinforced, went over to the attack again'; 'General Baggowut was thrown back at all points with the loss of his guns' (p. 117); 'into and over the ravine' (p. 118); 'reinforced by the Murom and the 2nd battalion of the Reval Musketeer Regiment and supported by a battery of General Ostermann, the Russian general went over the ravine again, threw the French back and retook the lost guns'; 'until General Somow with the Tula Musketeer Regiment, by a bayonet attack, decided the fight on this wing too in favour of the Russians, after darkness had already fallen'; 'that the Russians confined themselves to merely beating off the attacks of the French and nowhere carried out a counterstroke is explained by the exhaustion of the troops, by the state of the ground for movement, by the inadequate view of the enemy's strength in the bushy terrain, especially on the right wing, and by the fact that they wanted nothing other than to beat off an attack, which they also fully achieved with great economy of force'; '29 Russian battalions did not come into action at all'; Lannes, 'Marshal Lannes to the Emperor'; 'Pultusk, 27 December 1806'; 'as soon as I was formed, I had the enemy advance guard attacked by the 17th light and the 88th'; 'General Victor received the order to attack the left bridge with the 34th and a battalion of the 64th supported by the division Beker'; 'at the same time the enemy sent about 8,000 infantry and 3 cavalry regiments against my right, seeking to outflank me'; 'then I sent the rest of the 64th and the whole 88th against the right bridge to' (p. 463); 'cut off his retreat to the bridge, and I had him attacked by the 17th after a most lively fusillade' (p. 464); 'the enemy, seeing his left forced about 3 in the afternoon, detached a column from his right to try a second time to outflank our right, but the presence of General Gazan was enough to make it go back into line'; the journal, 'here are the operations of the 3rd division of the 3rd corps during the day of the 26th'; '(extract of the journal of operations of the 3rd corps)'; 'the general had all the battalions make a change of direction to the left, which gave him an oblique line on the enemy's flank'; 'the general deployment was carried out at once and the attack began immediately by half battalions and by echelons at 50 paces'.
No passage read gives side A's loss in the skirmishes with the Austrian outposts near Bregenz on 13 November and at Dornbirn on 14 November, and Bodart prints none. Unknown, not zero.

entries.claim_value: Höpfner: the three marshals, united at Schwerin, decided there on 4 November, given their superiority, to leave General Blücher no time to establish himself anywhere in a strong position; finding the position at Gadebusch abandoned on 5 November, Bernadotte followed directly by Rhena to Schönberg, while the Grand Duke of Berg and Soult turned left by Ratzeburg. Bernadotte wrote that he had agreed with Soult that Soult would march on Ratzeburg and he on Lübeck. Learning in the night that Swedes were about to embark, Bernadotte at once sent General Maison with some voltigeur companies, some guns and 100 horses to Schlutupp to interrupt the shipping on the Trave (Höpfner); at Schlutup he charged General Rouyer, with part of his brigade, to take the ships, then ordered him to sink them and throw troops onto the left bank to summon the Swedes (Bernadotte). Before Lübeck, though the enemy meant to defend the place and the ground gave him great advantages, Bernadotte did not hesitate to order the attack: Drouet's division, at the head, was to form by divisions and half-battalions and advance behind its voltigeurs, supported by guns; during the attack on the outer gate he ordered Rivaud to detach companies to take a bastion on the left; and once the town was taken he ordered Tilly to pass through it with the 3 light cavalry regiments and debouch. In Soult's corps Legrand's division was charged with the advanced work of the Mühlen gate, by Soult's order according to the Grand Duke of Berg, while Leval's division was directed on another gate and Saint-Hilaire's kept in reserve. The Grand Duke wrote that he marched in person with Soult and Lasalle's brigade, that he ordered the cavalry let through to pursue on the Travemünde road, and that d'Hautpoul had orders to summon Blücher. Soult wrote that the Grand Duke had principally directed the attacks; the Grand Duke, that no better dispositions could have been made than the marshals'. Höpfner: at the Mühlenthor, prisoners said that the Grand Duke commanded opposite.
entries.author_rationale: Side A's letters and side B's history, read from the page images. These were decisions taken in the action by side A's commanders, so the claim is tagged commander-created. The claim does not give the direction of the whole attack to one commander: Soult's and the Grand Duke's letters differ on it, and both are kept. English renderings (ours): 'the three marshals united at Schwerin had decided there on 4 November, given their superiority, to leave General Blücher no time to establish himself anywhere in a strong position'; 'when they therefore found the position at Gadebusch evacuated on 5 November and learned of the Prussians' retreat on Lübeck, Marshal Bernadotte followed at once directly from Gadebusch by Rhena to Schönberg, while the Grand Duke of Berg and Marshal Soult turned left by Ratzeburg'; 'Marshal Bernadotte to the major general. Lübeck, 7 November 1806'; 'I came to an understanding with Marshal Soult, and it was agreed that he would march on Ratzeburg and I on Lübeck'; 'still in the night to the 6th Marshal Bernadotte learned that a detachment of Swedes had withdrawn from Lauenburg to Lübeck and was about to embark at Travemünde'; 'he at once sent General Maison with some voltigeur companies, some guns and 100 horses to Schlutupp, with the order to interrupt the shipping on the Trave from there'; 'continuing our march we arrived at Schlutup, where we indeed saw on the Trave several ships ready to sail with Swedish troops, part of them already embarked, the others on the shore'; 'I charged General Rouyer, with part of his brigade, to make himself master of them'; 'but I ordered General Rouyer to sink the ships and at once throw some troops onto the left bank, summoning them to surrender if they did not want to be cut to pieces'; 'I soon recognised that the enemy meant to defend the place and that the locality gave him great advantages'; '[but, strong in the in]trepidity of our troops, I did not hesitate to order the attack'; 'I ordered Drouet's division, which was at the head, to form by divisions and half-battalions and to advance, preceded by its voltigeur companies and supported by some pieces of cannon that I at once had placed on the'; 'the inner gate was taken, but new resistance was met at the outer gate, which, like the rampart, was manned with infantry and defended by 2 pieces'; 'during the attack on this last gate I had ordered General Rivaud to detach some companies to take a bastion placed on the left while I had it battered by 2 pieces of artillery'; 'the 3 light cavalry regiments had also stayed there'; 'as soon as the town was in our power, I ordered General Tilly, who commanded them, to pass through it and debouch'; 'Marshal Soult to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806'; 'General Legrand's division was charged with carrying the advanced work of the Mühlen gate'; 'General Leval's division was at the same time directed on the Hertzberg gate, which it was also to carry; that of General Saint-Hilaire was in reserve'; 'His Imperial and Royal Highness the Grand Duke of Berg, who principally directed the attacks and who had brought up his cavalry to take part in them'; 'the Grand Duke of Berg to the Emperor. Lübeck, 6 November 1806, 9 o'clock in the evening'; 'I marched in person with Marshal Soult and General Lasalle's brigade'; 'then General Legrand received Marshal Soult's order to attack the advanced works of the Mühlen gate'; 'then I ordered the cavalry to be let through, which pursued the enemy at sword's point on the Travemünde road, by which General Blücher withdrew'; 'General d'Hautpoul has the order to summon General Blücher'; 'it is impossible to make better dispositions than those the Marshals made'; 'the Mühlenthor was attacked first, early on the 6th, by Marshal Soult and the Grand Duke of Berg'; 'prisoners stated that the Grand Duke of Berg commanded opposite, and the presence of much cavalry confirmed it'.

entries.claim_value: Side A attacked. In Moriggl, on 13 November the enemy attacked and pushed back the imperial outposts near Bregenz, and on the 14th French troops marched toward the Hohenems position, some detachments toward Staufen and the Bregenzerwald, and threw the Austrian outposts at Dornbirn out of the village and over the Dornbirner Ach, until Wolfskehl had the firing stopped; side B then capitulated. In Victoires, Augereau forced the Austrians to abandon Lindau and Bregenz and marched toward Feldkirch, and the Austrian general, soon surrounded, asked for a capitulation.
entries.author_rationale: Both accounts have side A advance on and surround side B, which capitulated without a battle; side B did not attack, so the code is A_attacked, and as the accounts agree it is one claim. Victoires says Augereau received the order to move onto the Vorarlberg to contain Jellachich's corps and push it onto the Tyrol (claim side-a-objectives). No passage read shows Augereau or Mathieu deciding at this engagement to attack: Moriggl names no commander for the attacks on the outposts or the turning detachments, and Augereau reached Bregenz only at noon on the 14th. So the posture is tagged inherited. English renderings (ours): as in claims side-a-command, moriggl-side-a, side-b-command and side-a-objectives.

No passage read gives a loss for side A, and Bodart prints none. Bodart has the garrison surrender without a stroke of the sword, and Höpfner says no shot had yet been fired when the council of war voted to surrender (claims bodart-strength, side-b-command); the skirmish before the gates on the eve, which the boundary note treats as context, is outside this count. No loss is stated, so it is left unknown, not set to zero.
